title: The Patient Sky
subtitle: A history of ancient astrology, and what it left standing
based_on: the documented history of Babylonian, Egyptian, Greek, Islamic, and medieval astrology and its entangled relationship with the birth of astronomy, mathematics, and medicine, plus an honest, clearly-flagged look at what controlled modern research has and has not found — ORIGINAL SYNTHESIS in the author's own words, not a derivative of any single existing popular-science book
author: Andries J. Greyling
protagonist: an ensemble cast of Babylonian scribes, Greek and Egyptian astronomer-astrologers, Islamic Golden Age scholars, and Renaissance astronomer-astrologers across three thousand years, narrated by a warm, funny, plain-spoken authorial voice (Bryson/Sapiens register)
setting: Uruk to Babylon to Alexandria to Baghdad to Prague, c. 1800 BCE-present
logline: Long before anyone could tell you whether astrology worked, the Chaldeans of Babylon were the first people on Earth to keep a dataset — night after night, tablet after tablet, cross-indexing the sky against harvests, plagues, and the moods of kings. That habit of patient, patterned watching outlived every specific prediction it ever made: it built the calendar, it built medicine's oldest curriculum, and — through the very telescopes and precise records astrology itself demanded — it built the science that eventually explained why the predictions didn't hold up.
blueprint: six-part chronological survey: (I) The Sky Before Names - Sumerian and Babylonian origins, the omen tablets, the invention of the zodiac; (II) The Chart Learns to Travel - Hellenistic diffusion, the birth of the horoscope, Ptolemy, Egypt, Rome; (III) The Same Hire - medical astrology from Hippocrates through the Islamic Golden Age to the medieval university curriculum, ending with Kepler moonlighting as a court astrologer; (IV) The Split - the telescope, Newton, the Enlightenment's line between astrology and astronomy, and what stayed behind (the calendar, the week, the zodiac's cultural residue); (V) Does Any of It Work? - Gauquelin, the Carlson double-blind study, precession, the psychology of why it still feels true, and astrology's modern commercial comeback; (VI) What Was Actually Built - astrology as humanity's first unified theory, a brief comparative look at Chinese and Vedic systems, and a closing chapter stating plainly what's real, what's open, and what's not supported
market: readers of Bill Bryson's A Short History of Nearly Everything, Yuval Noah Harari's Sapiens, Mary Beard, and this shelf's own Physics Won't Hurt You
status: DRAFT COMPLETE (26 ch across 6 parts + backmatter, ~43.6k, 2026-08-30)
tone: warm, funny, plain-spoken, unafraid of the strange; sympathetic to what astrology's practitioners were actually trying to do, while being honest and clearly-flagged throughout about what is documented history, what is a live open question, and what controlled study has specifically found not to hold up
dedication: For everyone who ever looked up and tried to make the pattern mean something. The looking was never the mistake.
clearances: All historical figures depicted are deceased and long-documented public figures of major historical record (Babylonian and Assyrian scribes and kings known from the cuneiform record, Berossus, Ptolemy, Hippocrates, al-Battani, al-Biruni, Kepler, Galileo, Newton, et al.) -> depictable. This is an ORIGINAL narrative synthesis built from the well-documented historical and scientific record; no sentence is copied from any existing popular-science book. No living person is named, quoted, or identifiably depicted anywhere in this book.
sensitivity_read: not required - historical/scientific record only, no living-person exposure. Modern astrology's commercial persistence (Chapter 23) is discussed as an industry and a psychological phenomenon, not through any named living practitioner or company.
